TO: O%ice of Public Participation

RE: Docket No. RM25-12-001 Docket No. PF25-11-000 and Docket No. CP26-80

FERC Commissioners,
CC O%ice of Public Participation Sta%

I am writing to oppose the proposed new rules on FERC's Blanket Certiﬁcate program
under Docket No. RM25-12-001. These new standards make blanket certiﬁcates bigger and
more dangerous, while doing nothing to protect our climate or communities. FERC is once
again acting as a rubber stamp and letting the fossil fuel industry run roughshod over the
public, the environment, and the public interest.

Two projects, in particular, show what is wrong with this new proposed rule: Argent LNG
and Project Jupiter's Green Chile Pipeline.

 Argent LNG is a Liqueﬁed Natural Gas export project, and would be the 2nd largest project
in Louisiana if built. It's also BP's ﬁrst deepwater drilling project since the deepwater
horizon spill more than 20 years ago. The LNG facility would be built in the fragile hurricane-
and ﬂood-prone Gulf Coast wetlands south of New Orleans. And the gas would come from
an existing network of deepwater drilling rigs in Gulf. But this is the most dangerous, "ultra
deep water" drilling with a huge impact on local wildlife and ecosystems.

Argent's owners and investors are trying to rush approval of the project with a blanket
certiﬁcate from FERC so they can eventually export more than 1.2 billion cubic feet of gas
per year by 2030. Every bit of it to be sold on the international market where it will drive
climate change, pollute the air, and drive up energy costs for US customers. Normally, a
project this big, this risky, and with this many potential impacts wouldn't qualify for a
blanket certiﬁcate, but FERC conveniently changed the rules in May to allow much bigger
projects to qualify and speciﬁcally said LNG facilities. This is what we mean when we say
you're a rubber stamp for industry.

 In addition, Energy Transfer (of Dakota Access Pipeline infamy) is asking for a blanket
certiﬁcate to build 18 miles of 24-inch diameter natural gas pipeline, which it calls Green
Chile. The pipeline itself is a problem, but the bigger issue is that Green Chile would only
have one customer: the massive Data center called Project Jupiter. Green Chile pipeline is
to supply the gas so that Project Jupiter can power itself with its very own ﬂeet of natural
gas power plants.
 But Project Jupiter is too big to be covered by any blanket certiﬁcate. The campus alone is
bigger than New York's Central Park, more than 1,400 acres. And those power-hungry data
centers could need as much as two-and-a-half gigawatts of electricity, more than the local
electric grid can possibly supply and more than half of what ﬂesh and blood New Mexicans
consume now. There are also concerns about the impacts on local wildlife, agriculture, and
water use in this drought-stricken part of the desert. Clearly, Green Chile is trying to sneak
a massive Data Center project with huge impacts on local electric customers, the
environment, and more through FERC by acting as if the pipeline is the only issue. It's not,
and FERC knows it. This is why we say you are dishonest and acting to suppress public
engagement and awareness of projects under your purview, when you should be focussing
on raising public awareness and making sure compliance with existing environmental and
consumer protection laws and regulations are followed.

 FERC should be looking for ways to stop all new fossil fuel infrastructure ‚—especially
expensive and wasteful projects like LNG export terminals and hyper-scale data centers
that will exacerbate the climate crisis, pollute our communities, and drive up costs for
consumers. And FERC should be looking for ways to expedite permitting and
interconnection of clean, renewable resources like solar, wind, and battery storage that will
reduce pollution, address the climate crisis, and which are already the cheapest way to
generate electricity anywhere in the world.

Sincerely,


drew Hudson
Rochester VT

documents.text:
FERC Commissioners,
CC Office of Public Participation Staff

On behalf of Beyond Extreme Energy, 198 methods, and Climate Hawks Vote Civic Action,
please accept the enclosed 11,791 comments on the proposed new rules on FERC's Blanket
Certificate program under Docket No. RM25-12-001. We are submitting the comments in bulk,
with individual vulgarities removed, as per your office’s request. I am also including photos of
the “blankets” BXE volunteers attempted to deliver at the July 16 Commissioners’ meeting. We
were advised by OPP staff at the time that delivering a photo through the E filing tool was more
practical than accepting receipt of the physical objects.

While each comment is unique and has been ccd independently to the Office of Public
Participation, I will summarize some common themes from these commenters for the record:

These new standards make blanket certificates bigger and more dangerous, while doing nothing
to protect our climate or communities. FERC is once again acting as a rubber stamp and letting
the fossil fuel industry run roughshod over the public, the environment, and the public interest.

Two projects, in particular, show what is wrong with this new proposed rule: Argent LNG and
Project Jupiter's Green Chile Pipeline.

Argent LNG is a Liquefied Natural Gas export project, and would be the 2nd largest project in
Louisiana if built. It's also BP's first deepwater drilling project since the deepwater horizon spill
more than 20 years ago. The LNG facility would be built in the fragile hurricane- and flood-prone
Gulf Coast wetlands south of New Orleans. And the gas would come from an existing network
of deepwater drilling rigs in the Gulf. But this is the most dangerous, "ultra deep water" drilling
with a huge impact on local wildlife and ecosystems.

Argent's owners and investors are trying to rush approval of the project with a blanket certificate
from FERC so they can eventually export more than 1.2 billion cubic feet of gas per year by
2030. Every bit of it to be sold on the international market where it will drive climate change,
pollute the air, and drive up energy costs for US customers. Normally, a project this big, this
risky, and with this many potential impacts wouldn't qualify for a blanket certificate, but FERC
conveniently changed the rules in May to allow much bigger projects to qualify and specifically
said LNG facilities. This is what we mean when we say you're a rubber stamp for industry.

In addition, Energy Transfer (of Dakota Access Pipeline infamy) is asking for a blanket
certificate to build 18 miles of 24-inch diameter natural gas pipeline, which it calls Green Chile.
The pipeline itself is a problem, but the bigger issue is that Green Chile would only have one
 customer: the massive Data center called Project Jupiter. Green Chile pipeline is to supply the
gas so that Project Jupiter can power itself with its very own fleet of natural gas power plants.

But Project Jupiter is too big to be covered by any blanket certificate. The campus alone is
bigger than New York's Central Park, more than 1,400 acres. And those power-hungry data
centers could need as much as two-and-a-half gigawatts of electricity, more than the local
electric grid can possibly supply and more than half of what flesh and blood New Mexicans
consume now. There are also concerns about the impacts on local wildlife, agriculture, and
water use in this drought-stricken part of the desert. Clearly, Green Chile is trying to sneak a
massive Data Center project with huge impacts on local electric customers, the environment,
and more through FERC by acting as if the pipeline is the only issue. It's not, and FERC knows
it. This is why we say you are dishonest and acting to suppress public engagement and
awareness of projects under your purview, when you should be focussing on raising public
awareness and making sure compliance with existing environmental and consumer protection
laws and regulations are followed.

FERC should be looking for ways to stop all new fossil fuel infrastructure—especially expensive
and wasteful projects like LNG export terminals and hyper-scale data centers that will
exacerbate the climate crisis, pollute our communities, and drive up costs for consumers. And
FERC should be looking for ways to expedite permitting and interconnection of clean,
renewable resources like solar, wind, and battery storage that will reduce pollution, address the
climate crisis, and which are already the cheapest way to generate electricity anywhere in the
world.

We hope that they commissioners, and the OPP staff will take the time to review each of these
comments individually, even though we are submitting them together in this format. Should you
have any questions, or wish to follow up with us about these comments, or any individual
commenter, please let us know and we will endeavor to provide the necessary information and
clarification.

Sincerely,

Drew Hudson on behalf of
Beyond Extreme Energy, BXE
198 methods
Climate Hawks Vote Civic Action
